new.headline: You ran 53 miles against a planned 37, and the long run drifted into tempo territory, so next week pulls the volume back a touch and puts the hard work in one marathon-pace session.

flags.title: Big volume jump

answers.question: I ran way more than the plan and felt fine. Can I keep this up?
answers.answer: Short answer: no, and I would not want you to. The jump from 24 to 37 to 53 miles in three weeks is roughly double the safe rate, and you only have six weeks left to turn this fitness into a marathon rather than build more of it. Feeling fine is normal in the week before an overuse problem shows up, not proof there isn't one. We will keep the honest gains from the 20 miler — that is a real long run in the bank — and spend the next three weeks turning strength into race-specific speed, then taper. If you keep tacking miles on, we lose the ability to hit marathon pace with fresh legs on Wednesdays, and the risk of a late-cycle injury climbs sharply.

new.analysis:
## What happened

Every single day went over plan, and the long run finished 5 miles long at a pace that put most of it in zone 3. The threshold session added a fourth rep because it felt good. These are all the same decision: trading recovery for extra work on a week where recovery was the point.

## Why that matters now

You are six weeks out from Wexley Lakes, and the next three weeks are where marathon pace lives. If you arrive at them with tired legs or a cranky calf, we lose the sessions that actually predict race day. The 20 miler was a good aerobic effort — keep it, do not chase it.

## What next week does

I am stepping total volume back a little to about 41 miles and moving the long run to 16 mi easy to let the system absorb last Sunday's effort. Wednesday is your first real marathon-pace workout: 5 miles at roughly 8:35/mi inside a 9-mile run. That is the specific stimulus you need, and it only works if the easy days around it are genuinely easy — zone 2, under 145 bpm, no bonus miles. Monday is rest. If the calf still complains on Tuesday, text me and we'll shorten Wednesday rather than skip it.

safetyCallouts.title: Watch the calves.
safetyCallouts.body: Tightness after a long run is normal, but if it turns into sharp pain, swelling or a limp, stop running and see a physio rather than training through it.
